extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, law, and civic theory (readers of Hobbes' Leviathan)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards for what counts as sin, crime, excuse, extenuation, and proper punishment in a commonwealth; guidance for distinguishing degrees of culpability and lawful punishment. Drawn from Hobbes' discussion of criminal responsibility, aggravation/mitigation, and the nature and limits of punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sinne (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Sinne is not only a transgression of a Law, but also any contempt of the Legislator; it may consist in commission, speaking forbidden words, omission of commanded acts, or in intention/purpose to transgress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intent alone (resolve to put an act in execution) can be sin, but mere imagination or dreaming (e.g., delighting in imagining another's goods or death) is not a sin under civil law; treating first motions of the mind as sins is overly severe.

rubrics_metrics.name: A Crime (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Crime is a sinne consisting in the committing (by deed or word) of that which the Law forbiddeth, or the omission of what it hath commanded; every Crime is a sinne, but not every sinne a Crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentions that never appear outwardly are sin before God but not subject to humane accusation; crime requires outward appearance of the intention (doctrine illustrated by Greek and Latin distinctions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Where No Civill Law Is, There Is No Crime
rubrics_metrics.description: If civil law ceaseth, Crimes cease: without civil law there is no place for accusation; actions contrary to natural law remain sine but not 'crime' in the civil sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sovereign power ceaseth, crime also ceaseth for those who did not contribute to the removal of that power; in such cases self-preservation by force is allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance Of The Law Of Nature Excuseth No Man
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance of the Law of Nature excuseth no man because every reasonable person is supposed to know not to do to another what he would not have done to himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching false or subversive doctrines that tend to disobedience is a crime even if the teacher believes them true; natural law obligations travel with the use of reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance Of The Civill Law Excuseth Sometimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance of civil law excuses a man in a strange country until the law is declared to him; where civil law is not sufficiently declared so a man cannot know it, ignorance is a good excuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of declaration or accessibility of civil law can excuse; mere lack of diligence does not count as lack of means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance Of The Soveraign Excuseth Not
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance of the sovereign power in the place of a man's ordinary residence excuses him not; he ought to take notice of the power that has protected him there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Residents are held responsible to know and obey the sovereign authority under which they live.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance Of The Penalty Excuseth Not
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance of the penalty, where the law is declared, excuseth no man; punishment is a known consequence of violating laws and is accepted by voluntary action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If penalty is determined by law, the offender is subject to it even if ignorant; if not determined, discretionary punishment may follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishments Declared Before The Fact, Excuse From Greater Punishments After It
rubrics_metrics.description: When a penalty is annexed to the crime in the law itself, or has been usually inflicted, the delinquent is excused from a greater punishment inflicted after the fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a foreknown but insufficient punishment invites the crime (actors compare benefit vs punishment), inflicting a greater penalty than foreknown is unjust and counts as the law tempting men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nothing Can Be Made A Crime By A Law Made After The Fact
rubrics_metrics.description: No law made after a fact can make it a crime; a positive law cannot be obligatory before it is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a law forbidding a fact is made before the fact, the actor is liable to the penalty ordained after if no lesser penalty had been known before by writing or example.

rubrics_metrics.name: False Principles Of Right And Wrong Causes Of Crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Defects in reasoning (error) lead men to violate laws by adopting false principles: e.g., 'Justice is but a vain word', or that success authorizes injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such false principles remove moral constraint and make acts legal/vicious depending on fortune rather than law; they are a source of crime rooted in erroneous reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: False Teachers Mis-interpreting The Law Of Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: False teachers who misinterpret the law of nature, or teach doctrines/traditions inconsistent with a subject's duty, are causes of crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority of teachers can spread error; the community may be taught to act contrary to lawful duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erroneous Inferences From True Principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Hasty or precipitate persons draw erroneous inferences from true principles, leading to crime; this is common among those overconfident in their natural wit without study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such error may mitigate but cannot fully excuse crime for those managing private business, and especially not for public officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions As Causes (Vain-glory, Presumption, Anger, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Passions such as vain-glory, presumption of riches or friends, overrating of one's wisdom, hatred, lust, ambition, covetousness, and anger incline men to break the law and produce crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These passions make men expect impunity or encourage deceit; they often require extraordinary use of reason or consistent punishment to be restrained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption Of Riches and Friends Aggravates Crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Presumption of riches or multitude of potent kindred and friends encourages violation of laws on hope of escaping punishment, and thus aggravates the crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crimes motivated by presumed ability to corrupt justice or resist execution are worse than opportunistic crimes by those who fear being discovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wisedome (false opinion of one's wisdom) Aggravates Certain Crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: A false high opinion of one's wisdom leads to crimes of craft and deceit and to public disturbance by calling authority into question; such presumption aggravates crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who unsettle laws by public discourse or craft are especially culpable; many chief movers of commonwealth disturbance fail to enjoy the fruits of their designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear As Cause: Corporeal Fear May Excuse, Phantastic Fear Does Not
rubrics_metrics.description: Only present bodily fear that leaves no way of escape may justify an action (e.g., killing in self-defence); fears of non-corporeal or future/phantastic harms (e.g., shame, dreams, visions) do not excuse and count as crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Killing to avert immediate bodily danger is not a crime; killing out of apprehension of future danger or reputation is a crime. Superstitious fears or following dreams as justification are not accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crimes Not Equall — room for Excuse and Extenuation
rubrics_metrics.description: All crimes are not of the same alloy; there is place for total excuse (removing the obligation of law) and for extenuation (making a great crime less), so crimes differ in degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stoic view that all crimes are equal is rejected; the law should account for differences in culpability and harmfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totall Excuses (criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Total excuses that remove the nature of a crime include lack of means to know the law, children and madmen excused from natural law offences, captivity or being in an enemy's power without fault, compulsion by present terror of death, and necessity (e.g., famine taking food).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Want of means to learn the law removes obligation; voluntary lack of diligence does not. Obedience to enemy or compulsion to preserve life are total excuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excuses Against The Author (acting by authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts done against the law by the authority of another are excused with respect to the author (since one should not accuse his own fact in another) but not excused as to third persons injured; sovereign commands contrary to former law totally excuse the actor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If sovereign or assembly commands contrary to former law, the command as to that fact abrogates the prior law and excuses obedience; but refusal to obey granted liberties inconsistent with sovereignty may be a sin and crime if resisted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees Of Crime (four measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degrees of crime are measured by (1) the malignity of the source or cause, (2) the contagion of the example, (3) the mischief of the effect, and (4) the concurrence of times, places, and persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four axes should be used to determine how much greater or lesser a crime is compared to the same act in different circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption Of Power Aggravates
rubrics_metrics.description: The same fact is a greater crime if it proceeds from presumption of strength, riches, or friends (presumption of impunity by force) than if done from hope of escaping by flight or error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presumption of impunity is a root of contempt of all laws and indicates greater likelihood of repeat offenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evill Teachers Extenuate
rubrics_metrics.description: Error that proceeds from the authority of a publicly authorized teacher or interpreter of law is less faulty and may excuse totally in cases not denying sovereign power or against evident law; private judgement errors are less excusable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What is taught by public authority resembles law until contradicted by sovereign authority; reliance on such instruction mitigates culpability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples Of Impunity Extenuate
rubrics_metrics.description: Constant examples of impunity in others for the same act extenuate the offender's culpability because the sovereign's prior tolerance furnishes hope of impunity and shares blame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If those in power have given hope of mercy or impunity, the offender cannot be reasonably charged with the whole fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praemeditation Aggravates
rubrics_metrics.description: A crime arising from long meditation is worse than one from sudden passion; premeditation involves conscious contempt of law, punishment, and consequences to society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sudden passion may mitigate somewhat but does not totally excuse; the time between knowing the law and acting is taken as time for deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tacite Approbation Of The Soveraign Extenuates
rubrics_metrics.description: Where law condemns an act but the lawmaker's tacit approval appears (through practice, example, or discouraging penalty for conformity), the act is a lesser crime because the sovereign's approbation partly causes the transgression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulers should avoid tacit encouragement of acts they forbid; the example of princes is powerful in shaping behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison Of Crimes From Their Effects (harm to many and reputational effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: The same fact is a greater crime when it harms many rather than few, when it harms by present and future contagious example, and when committed by persons whose reputation or office makes their example influential (preacher, professor, public official).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider multiplicative 'fertility' of a crime through example and the special culpability of those whose actions teach others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laesae Majestas (crimes against the commonwealth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hostile acts against the state (betraying strengths, revealing secrets, attempts upon representative authority, words or deeds diminishing authority) are greater crimes and understood as crimes of laesae majestas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These acts damage the whole commonwealth and are treated as crimes against fundamental law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bribery And False Testimony As Greater Crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Crimes that render judgments of no effect (taking money for false judgment or testimony) are greater because they attack all judgments and enable force and private vengeance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrupting justice has systemic effects and so is treated more severely than equivalent private frauds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depeculation (robbery of public treasure) Is Greater
rubrics_metrics.description: Robbery and embezzlement of public treasure or revenues is a greater crime than robbing a private man because it robs many at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public theft undermines the commonwealth's resources and harms many citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfeiting Public Authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterfeiting usurpation of public ministry, public seals, or public coin is a greater crime than counterfeiting a private person's seal, because the fraud extends to the damage of many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usurpation and counterfeit of public signs attack the trust infrastructure of society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crimes Against Private Men Compared (hierarchy of harms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative ranking of private harms: killing > other injury; killing with torment > simple killing; mutilation of a limb > spoiling goods; spoiling goods by terror/wounds > clandestine surreption > fraud by consent; rape by force > by flattery; married woman violated > unmarried.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also aggravated: killing a parent greater than killing another; robbing the poor is worse than robbing the rich; crimes in places/times of devotion are worse—law values general human sensitivities, not idiosyncrasies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public vs Private Crimes (pleas)
rubrics_metrics.description: A crime is 'publique' when the accusation is in the name of the commonwealth and 'private' when in the name of a private person; pleas are named accordingly (Judicia Publica, Pleas of the Crown vs Private Pleas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public prosecutions reflect injury to the commonwealth beyond the private victim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition Of Punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: A PUNISHMENT is an evill inflicted by publique Authority on him that hath done or omitted that which is judged by the same Authority to be a transgression of the law, to the end that the will of men may thereby be disposed to obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment's proper end is future disposition to obedience; it is not mere revenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right To Punish Whence Derived
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of punishing in a commonwealth stems from the pre-societal right every man had to preserve himself; subjects did not grant the sovereign the right but strengthened the sovereign's own right to use force as he thinks fit for preservation (limited by natural law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereign punishment is rooted in the sovereign's retained power to preserve subjects, not a delegated gift from subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private Injuries and Revenges Are Not Punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Private revenges or injuries of private men are not properly 'punishment' because they do not proceed from public authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only evils inflicted by public authority after public judgment count as punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial Of Preferment Is Not Punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Neglect or non-preferment by public favour is not punishment, because it inflicts no new evil—only leaves one in prior estate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment implies an inflicted evil, not mere withholding of favour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pain Inflicted Without Publique Hearing Is Not Punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Evil inflicted by public authority without prior public condemnation is not 'punishment' but an act of hostility; punishment requires antecedent public judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due process (public condemnation) is part of what distinguishes punishment from arbitrary violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pain Inflicted By Usurped Power Is Not Punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Evil inflicted by usurped power or judges without authority is not punishment but an act of hostility because such acts lack legitimate authorizing sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illegitimate exercise of force cannot be called lawful punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pain Inflicted Without Respect To The Future Good Is Not Punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Any evil inflicted without intention or possibility of disposing the delinquent or by example others to obey laws is hostility, not punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment must have the prospective aim of reforming or deterring; mere harm without that aim is not lawful punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturall Evill Consequences Are Not Punishments (by men)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural evil consequences (illness, being slain in an assault) are not 'punishments' in the human/mundane sense because they are not inflicted by human authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such consequences may be divine punishment but not civil punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hurt Less Than Benefit Is Not Punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: If the harm inflicted is less than the benefit or contentment that naturally follows the crime, that harm is not punishment but rather price or redemption, because it fails the end of disposing men to obey the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment must be sufficient to deter; otherwise it functions as a cost paid for the crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where The Punishment Is Annexed To The Law, A Greater Hurt Inflicted After Is Hostility
rubrics_metrics.description: If a punishment is prescribed by law and after the crime a greater punishment is inflicted, the excess is not punishment but an act of hostility; where no punishment was previously determined, whatever is inflicted has the nature of punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-retroactive imposition of harsher penalties is unjust; declared punishments are the measure of lawful retribution.
